data.title: Daily Markets Briefing: STI up 0.49%; Top stock is Singtel

data.title: Treat AI agents as shoppers, not bankers: Google's Jeremy Goro
data.description:
AI agents must not invent a shadow financial system.

Deploying AI agents in the financial industry must involve strict boundaries where they are just shoppers and not bankers.

“AI agents must speak the language of these [payment] rails, not invent a shadow financial system,” Jeremy Goro, head of financial services strategy & partnerships, EMEA at Google, told attendees of the Policy Stage of Singapore Fintech Festival 2026 on 19 November.

AI agents must be trusted expert shoppers, not shadow bankers, Goro said in a panel moderated by Jo Yeon, a director at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

Goro emphasized the need to establish clear technical boundaries for AI, and for payment execution and Know-Your-Customer to remain with licensed banks, established payment networks, and payment service providers, Goro said.

“We need to preserve the established liability and consumer protections because innovation cannot come at the expense of consumer rights,” Goro said.

Goro said that the industry must work to have tamper-proof cryptographic electronic sign mandates for autonomous commerce. This meant having strict limits like a maximum price, merchant criteria, and expiration timeline for AI agents executing a transaction.

“The real opportunity lies in anchoring autonomous AI directly into trusted national rails and consumer protections that have already been protecting billions of users every day,” Goro said.

Goro was joined at the panel by Kelvin Li, senior vice president at Ant International, and Jesse McWaters, EVP, head of global policy at Mastercard.

Li expects agentic AI payments to make up 50% of all payment activity by 2030 and it will be normalized enough that “payments will just happen,” Li said.

“Previously, we were looking at payments from a transaction perspective. So now we will be looking at a task perspective,” Li said.

Li said that the future payment system will need to be able to handle cross-border nanopayments.

McWaters, meanwhile, warned that inadequate liability and fraud protections may discourage banks and merchants from accepting AI agent transactions. But he also asked regulators to approach agentic commerce not just with risk in mind but also to consider the opportunities.

“In many cases, I think what's really required in order to deliver on that is thinking about how those regulations and that guidance should be evolved to meet the needs of an evolving ecosystem, rather than trying to  slap some new regulations on top of the existing frameworks,” McWaters said.

data.title: Payment networks face governance hurdles in cross-border expansion
data.description:
Executives flag pricing, dispute and fraud concerns across different jurisdictions. 

Differences in payment rules, commercial incentives, and dispute procedures are complicating efforts to connect national payment networks across borders, executives said at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 19 November.

Joyce Bo, executive vice president for core payments in Asia Pacific at Mastercard, said national QR payment schemes typically use push payments, whilst card networks and many mobile wallets rely on pull payments.

These systems have different messaging, authentication and settlement models, requiring technical integration alongside common commercial and regulatory arrangements, she said in a panel discussion.

Moreover, payment operators must reconcile differences in pricing, merchant arrangements and dispute rules to make cross-border connections commercially sustainable.

"Every participant needs to have the right incentives, and consumers need to continue to be protected," she added.

Andrew McCormack, CEO of Nexus Global Payments, said connecting payment systems also requires a common framework establishing the roles and responsibilities of participating institutions.

"Nexus is a technology platform, but probably more importantly, it's a scheme rule book," he said.

McCormack said the framework covers dispute resolution and how the network interacts with domestic systems such as India's Unified Payments Interface and Singapore's PayNow and FAST.

He added that banks and payment service providers remain responsible for authenticating their customers, whilst disputes involving fraud, human error or technical failures require established procedures.

Carlos Álvarez, chief risk officer at FLAR, said cross-border connections introduce additional participants, including foreign exchange and settlement providers, which can create operational risks.

"For instance, in smaller markets, will these providers be reliable and able to provide the services 24/7 and the like?" Álvarez said.

He also raised concerns about differences in how jurisdictions prevent fraud and recover funds. "Because in practice, what happens when there is a risk is that you have different standards for dealing with fraud, right? So the level of maturity between countries is different.”

Meanwhile, Mike Truter, head of industry engagement at Swift, identified regulatory reporting obligations, capital and foreign exchange controls, and inconsistent market practices as major obstacles in the final stage of cross-border payments.

He said addressing these issues requires coordinated action amongst policymakers, payment infrastructure operators, financial institutions and technology providers.

"It's not as simple as one pays; everyone has to pay. Everyone plays the game," Truter said.

Sohini Rajola, executive director for growth at the National Payments Corporation of India, said the commercial design of cross-border connections should prioritise reducing costs for consumers and merchants before determining how expenses are shared.

She said intermediaries must find ways to make transactions faster and cheaper without passing additional costs to end users.

"If there are incentives which don't align for that, you can have anything on paper as a blueprint. It's not going to be able to succeed or scale," Rajola said.

Despite these challenges, payment networks are pursuing additional international connections.

McCormack said Nexus plans to begin a pilot involving Singapore and Malaysia in 2027, followed by India and other participating markets.

Álvarez also highlighted Project Lumina, which is working with five Latin American central banks to assess the technical, regulatory and commercial requirements for future cross-border payment integration.

data.title: Financial firms must rein in AI agents with identity checks and audit trails
data.description:
Speed, autonomy and unclear responsibility set the technology apart from past automation.

Industry leaders said financial institutions using artificial intelligence (AI) agents should give each agent an identity, limit what it can do and keep a tamper-proof record of its actions.

Kenneth Gay, chief fintech officer at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the organisation released a Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime framework earlier this year.

“Industry good practice would form the basis for firmer supervisory and regulatory guidelines, as MAS did with its recent AI risk guidelines,” he said during a panel session at the Singapore FinTech Festival.

Gay added that MAS also unveiled an agentic finance sandbox and is working on a protocol for agentic transactions alongside it.

He said agents act autonomously and can go beyond their instructions. “For example, an agent buying an item might pick expedited shipping to get it there sooner or order the wrong colour”.

Gay said the challenge for the industry is to allow meaningful control whilst leaving agents room to improve outcomes by reasoning and interacting with other agents or services.

Mahesh Uttamchandani, regional practice director for digital and AI at the World Bank Group, said human in the loop has become a cliché, and that the real question is where to place the human.

“Agents will execute subtasks, set their own guidance and interact with other agents, which calls for circuit breakers and immutable audit trails so that investigators can reconstruct what happened and who bears responsibility for mistakes,” Uttamchandani said.  

Daniela Stoffel, state secretary at SIF, said agents must be identified and tied to liability, accountability or authentication, because every economic action rests on ownership, responsibility and transparency. “I don’t think we have full awareness of the complexity,” she said.

Jonah Crane, head of global regulatory and policy strategy at Stripe, noted that automation is not new in the sector.

He cited high-frequency trading, which has existed for about 25 years, as well as automated credit underwriting and insurance claims processing.

Claude Marx, director general at CSSF Luxembourg, said the difference this time is speed, with several frontier AI models now released each year and agents that can be combined.

He said keeping humans in the loop and maintaining auditability are the challenges, and that both will become harder as quantum computing arrives, which he estimated is two to three years away from becoming mainstream.

Marx added that regulators will need data scientists and analysts at a senior level to become data-driven supervisors.

data.title: Financial firms strengthen safeguards to scale AI beyond pilots
data.description:
AI payments need banks, merchants and tech firms to support agent-initiated transactions.

Financial firms are embedding safeguards into artificial intelligence (AI) systems, preparing payment networks, and training employees as they seek to expand AI beyond pilot projects, executives said at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 19 November.

Speaking at a panel discussion, Abhijeet Ramesh, vice president and head of innovation and growth for Asia Pacific at Visa, said scaling AI-powered payments requires banks, merchants, and technology firms to support transactions initiated by AI agents.

“True scale comes from getting the whole ecosystem activated,” he said.

Ramesh cited Visa's Agentic Ready programme, which has enabled about 100 banks in the Asia Pacific to recognise and process agent-initiated transactions.

The company has also introduced an initiative to prepare merchants to accept such transactions and is working with partners to expand the reach of its Visa Intelligent Commerce service, he added.

Meanwhile, Mayoran Rajendra, managing director and general manager of the AI Transformation Department at SMBC, said financial firms must establish governance controls early, particularly as AI systems can produce different outputs.

Rajendra said SMBC has incorporated evaluations, traceability and controls into the business requirements of its AI applications, rather than introducing these measures after development.

“Think there is a very smart intern who joins your team. How would you teach them how to do the job? How would you give the guidance? Work within which parameters and within the range,” he added.

The bank has also worked with its risk management team and engaged with the Monetary Authority of Singapore on AI governance.

“Greater clarity will help us understand how far we can go, accelerate AI deployment, and provide assurance to our employees,” he said.

For UOB, workforce preparation has been another part of expanding AI adoption.

Janet Young, managing director and group head of channels and digitalisation, strategic communications and brand at UOB, said the bank has expanded Microsoft Copilot access from several thousand employees to all 32,000 staff.

The bank has also invested in employee development programmes to help staff adopt the solution in their work. “They can now be freed up to do things that are of value,” she said.

UOB has also expanded AI-powered surveillance in private banking through Project Magnet, increasing transaction monitoring from 5% manual sampling to 100% of transactions.

Meanwhile, Quan Yu, senior vice president at Ant International, said the company is exploring how AI agents can take on more responsibilities in credit policy and lending decisions.

The company is developing agents to support data analysis, credit policies and risk assessments, although Yu said determining how much decision-making to delegate to AI remains a challenge.

Ant International continues to use human checks and A/B testing to assess automated decisions, particularly to ensure individual borrowers are treated fairly.

“For now, for those decisions, we still do A/B testing,” Yu said, adding that the company also checks whether the results meet expectations.

data.title: StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered complete tokenised deposit payment test
data.description:
US dollar payments can now be settled within minutes and outside conventional banking hours.

StraitsX, OCBC and Standard Chartered have completed a test using tokenised deposits issued by different banks for payments between financial institutions, settling US dollar payments within minutes outside conventional banking hours.

The proof of concept, carried out under the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s BLOOM initiative, addresses a growing challenge as banks build their own tokenised deposit ecosystems.

Because tokenised deposits are claims only against the bank that issues them, they cannot be moved easily between different banks’ ecosystems, which may run on different platforms and standards.

The test used StraitsX’s shared settlement infrastructure to coordinate payments across OCBC’s and Standard Chartered’s tokenised deposit ecosystems, covering payment initiation, compliance screening, liquidity checks, settlement and confirmation. Tokenised deposits from both banks were treated as equivalent within the shared framework.

“Tokenised deposits have the potential to enable near-instant and programmable money movement, but their broader utility will depend on how effectively different banking ecosystems can connect,” said Tianwei Liu, CEO and co-founder of StraitsX.

Many traditional interbank US dollar payments run within fixed settlement windows and are unavailable outside business hours. In the test, payments settled outside conventional cut-off times, with compliance, liquidity and settlement processes completed within minutes.

The participants also found the shared model reduced the need for bilateral prefunding between institutions, pointing to more efficient liquidity management than conventional models.

Broader rollout will require further work on legal, regulatory, operational and commercial arrangements, including settlement finality, liquidity management, participant responsibilities and financial crime controls.

Any commercial implementation remains subject to regulatory engagement, participant approvals, legal documentation and operational risk assessments.

data.title: Banks plan own digital money but industry leaders question the odds
data.description:
JP Morgan and Ripple doubt bank consortia can scale tokenised deposits.

Banks are choosing tokenised deposits over stablecoins, but industry leaders are questioning whether bank consortia can deliver them at scale.

Speaking at a panel discussion at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 19 November, Umar Farooq, global co-head of payments at J.P. Morgan, said banks are forming groups because stablecoins pull liquidity out of the banking system.  

Farooq pointed to a 21-bank group on the dollar side, a European consortium, and Project Agora, which involves central banks.

“Such groups are building closed systems, which is a good first step but not a feasible end solution”, he said. Banks would eventually need to accept each other’s tokenised assets, he added.

Brad Garlinghouse, chief executive of Ripple, was blunter, calling the bank consortia ‘almost dead on arrival '. He said this opens room for fast-moving, nimble players.  

Ralph Hamers, chairman of Banking Circle, said trust is the basis of any such arrangement. “Everything happens only because there is trust,” he said.

On the stablecoin side, Farooq said the market stood at around $300b on 1 January and is at the same level today. “If this thing were explosive, you would see the stock go up through the roof,” he added.

Hamers cited McKinsey figures showing stablecoin volume has doubled in two years but accounts for only 0.02% of all money moving globally. Garlinghouse read the same figure as headroom. “That’s all opportunity,” he said.

Farooq said J.P. Morgan’s Kinexys platform processes more than $2 trillion in business-to-business transactions annually, which he described as much bigger than stablecoin volumes in that segment.

Use cases include weekend foreign exchange settlement for payment service providers in Asia, which avoids pre-funding, and margin payments for oil and gas companies when US markets are closed.

Meagen Burnett, chief financial officer at Schroders, said the asset manager will not issue a stablecoin, offer payments, or tokenise deposits.

“Because stablecoins pay no yield, Schroders instead launched a tokenised money market fund with J.P. Morgan through the Central Bank of Ireland, with corporate treasury as the next target,” she added.

Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said traditional and crypto players are increasingly collaborating, citing DBS’s announcement a day earlier that it is working with Circle.

Hamers said he expects consolidation amongst the growing number of rails and currencies.  

Farooq added that faster rails also raise the stakes if trading becomes automated. “There are no new problems—there are always old problems that are augmented because of new technology,” he said, adding that circuit breakers would be needed if agentic trading grows.

He also warned that markets will eventually face a discontinuity, as in 2022, with quite negative outcomes if everything is automated, tokenised and running around the clock.

data.title: Standard Chartered rolls out tokenised deposits in Singapore
data.description:
This builds on its launch of tokenised deposit services in Hong Kong.

Standard Chartered has launched its tokenised deposits solution in Singapore, built on its proprietary blockchain infrastructure,

This is expected to enable near real-time transactions across Singapore and Hong Kong, the bank said on 19 November 2026.

Eligible clients can utilised their commercial bank deposits within digital treasury and investment workflows, including intragroup liquidity management, Standard Chartered said.

The solution supports multiple currencies including SGD, HKD, USD, EUR, CNH, GBP.

Standard Chartered rolled out tokenised deposits in Hong Kong on 2 November.

Companies that have made live tokenised deposit transactions include China AMC, Finloop, and PantherTrade, Standard Chartered Hong Kong said. It is also working with Fireblocks and Hashkey to expand the reach of its tokenised deposit solution.

Earlier in 2026, Standard Chartered bought Zodia Custody, a digital asset custody business.

data.title: Mastercard and Ant test AI agent business payments in Singapore
data.description:
It aims to verify AI agents' identity and permissions for consumer and business transactions.

Mastercard and Ant International have completed a Singapore pilot that tested how businesses can securely authorise AI agents to purchase digital services within predefined spending limits, as the companies also demonstrated a live consumer AI payment in Asia Pacific.

The two completed an Agent Pay for Machines (AP4M) pilot with Antom in Singapore, testing how businesses can allow AI agents to make purchases whilst maintaining control over spending limits and approved activities.

The pilot allowed an AI agent to use credentials, policy controls and payment authorisation features to purchase digital services within parameters set by the business.

Meanwhile, the companies conducted a live consumer transaction through Antom, Ant International’s merchant payment and digitalisation platform, where an AI agent purchased a cup of coffee based on a consumer’s pre-approved intent.

The transaction used Mastercard Agent Pay with Verifiable Intent, which creates a record of what the consumer authorised the AI agent to do.

The technology combines network tokenisation, authentication and consumer intent verification to support agent-initiated payments.

The move comes as AI agents become more involved in commerce. Mastercard said establishing trust around identity and authority will be critical to wider adoption.

“AI agents are already capable of completing payments. The bigger challenge now is creating the trust for consumers, businesses and merchants to embrace them,” said Joyce Bo, executive vice president, Core Payments, Asia Pacific, Mastercard.

The companies said the collaboration aims to help merchants accept purchases from AI agents acting within consumer- or business-approved permissions, whilst enabling new AI-driven commerce models.

“Trust creates a foundation for merchants to rethink how they deliver value, from reaching more customers through AI agents to offering services in smaller, flexible units that agents can discover, combine and purchase,” said Chunmao Zhu, vice president, Technology & Business, Antom.

The developments come as companies explore how AI agents could move beyond assisting users to directly carrying out tasks such as shopping, payments and business procurement.

data.title: Visa and Alipay+ expand QR payment access for Singapore travellers
data.description:
Users can pay at Alipay+ merchants with linked Visa cards.

Visa has rolled out its Scan to Pay service with Alipay+, allowing eligible Visa cardholders to pay at participating QR merchants across Asia Pacific, including Singapore.

The service allows travellers to use their Visa credentials through participating digital wallets to scan and pay at Alipay+ merchants without downloading a separate local payment application.

Under the arrangement, Google Wallet users from supported markets can use eligible Visa cards to scan and pay at participating Alipay+ merchants when travelling to Singapore.

Samsung Wallet users in Singapore and Australia can also use eligible Visa cards to pay at participating Alipay+ merchants in Hong Kong and Malaysia.

The service is enabled by Visa Pay, which supports interoperable QR payments through digital wallets and banking applications.

It allows participating wallet providers to extend the international acceptance of Visa credentials whilst retaining their existing customer-facing applications.

Visa said it plans to expand the rollout to more wallet users and destination markets as the partnership develops.
